claims.text: A hybrid ML-accelerated thermodynamic-integration method with on-the-fly ab initio corrections can accurately evaluate solid and liquid free energies while substantially reducing computational cost.
The method is intended for elemental, binary, and multicomponent high-entropy alloys near fusion conditions.
Accurate near-fusion free energies require vibrational, anharmonic, and electron-vibration coupling effects to be included.
The ML potential will be trained on a sparse set of ab initio calculations covering both solid and liquid phases.
Active learning will periodically select additional ab initio calculations to correct the ML potential during thermodynamic integration.
The proposed operating range is approximately 0.8 to 1.2 times the melting temperature.
The method can ultimately be extended to high-entropy alloys with up to 5–7 principal elements.
The ML potential can map the relevant free-energy landscape across solid-liquid phase boundaries.
ML interatomic potentials can approximate underlying DFT energies and forces at much lower computational cost.
Selected on-the-fly ab initio recalculations will keep the ML approximation accurate throughout thermodynamic integration.
The hybrid procedure will accurately retain vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron-vibration coupling.
The method is expected to provide up to an order-of-magnitude speedup over explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics free-energy workflows.
The method is expected to be 2–3 times faster than TOR-TILD for high-entropy systems.
The method will maintain free-energy errors below 0.01 eV per atom.
Explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics free-energy calculations are highly accurate but computationally expensive.
Elemental and binary systems can serve as initial validation cases before extension to multicomponent alloys.
The exact speedup, error margin in extreme compositional spaces, and robustness of active learning remain uncertain.

A decisive benchmark will compare solid and liquid phase free energies, melting temperature, latent heat, and entropy of fusion against fully explicit ab initio molecular dynamics in a well-characterized binary alloy.
The hypothesis is falsified if free-energy deviations exceed 0.01 eV per atom or the method fails to achieve an order-of-magnitude speedup over explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
